In this vignette we will walk through the process of loading a housepi model template.
Then we will explain how to associate necessary definitions in order to perform inference and simulations.

# Format of the data

Data can be provided as a numerical data.frame in wide format, where individual information are organised by row.
A simplistic dataset would look something like^[
Note that this dataset comes automatically with the model "blank", used for testing mode.]

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">
<div>

```{r}
#| label: blank-data-table
#| echo: false
env <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
utils::data("blank_house", package = "housepi", envir = env)
knitr::kable(env[["blank_house"]])
```

</div>
</div>

The housepi package comes with a few public datasets to be used for testing.

A column `"id"` with individual identifiers is provided to keep track of changes and make errors more readable; otherwise housepi will automatically tag individuals with row numbers.

To group individuals in households, a column `"house_id"` with the respective household tag needs to be present.
Individuals with the same household id will then be considered to belong to same household.
No household id implies that all individuals in the data are living separately.

To perform model inference, a `"status"` must be provided for each individual $i$.
Status $s_{i}$ should be an integer value satisfying the following convention:

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">
<div>

| Status $s_{i}$ | Compartment | Serology     |
|:--------------:|-------------|--------------|
| $\geq$ `1`     | infectious  | seropositive |
| `0`            | susceptible | seronegative |
| `NA`           | missing     | missing      |

</div>
</div>

In this way we can use the status as a label for different classes of infectious household members.
E.g. we could say that $s_{i} = 1$ refers to symptomatic individuals, and $s_{i} = 2$ for asymptomatic.
This is used in advanced augmented definitions, see [Data augmentation](data_augmentation.html) for an example.

# The housepi model class

The central element of the package is the [R6 class](https://r6.r-lib.org/articles/Introduction.html) `HousepiModel`.
A dataset in wide format must be provided at model construction via the `data` argument of `new_housepi_model()`. 

We show how to generate a new instance of such a class with a template model, the chain binomial:

```{r}
#| label: load-model
# import the library housepi
library(housepi)
# set general seed
set.seed(42)
# set the theme for visualizations
housepi_theme_set()

# generate an instance of the chain binomial model with data
hhmodel <- new_housepi_model(flu_1918_frederick, "chain_binomial")
```

We can retrieve the template model description by using the method `$help()`.

A brief summary of the loaded data can be obtained via `summarise_cases()`,
here manipulated with [flextable](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=flextable):

```{r}
#| label: summarise-cases
# show a summary of cases as a `flextable`
summarise_cases(hhmodel) |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::set_formatter(pct = function(x) round(x, 1)) |>
  flextable::merge_v(j = ~ type) |>
  flextable::bold(j = ~ type + comment, bold = TRUE) |>
  flextable::labelizor(labels = c(type = "", comment = "", pct = "[%]")) |>
  flextable::autofit()
```

At any moment we can re-export the full data by calling `$data_wide`.

```{r}
#| label: import-data
# data was associated to the model at construction above
head(hhmodel$data_wide)
```

# A collection of models

To see the complete list of available template models, from within RStudio just run

```{r}
#| label: list-templates
# present the list of template model name
browse_housepi_templates()
```

Each template comes with its template definitions that can be used straight away or changed^[Note that in names both underscores and spaces are accepted, i.e. "chain_binomial" is equivalent to "chain binomial".].
To know more about each model, choose a name from the previous list and run, e.g.

```{r}
#| label: model-help
#| eval: false
# show model description in RStudio help window
browse_housepi_templates("chain_binomial")
```

This command will open the relative documentation file in the Help window of your RStudio session.
Our project aims at expanding the present collection of templates, in order to improve off-the-shelf analysis.

# Associate parameters

Here we show how to provide a single parameter definition (prior and proposal needed for the Bayesian Monte Carlo).
We can call `add_parameter()` as follows:

```{r}
#| label: add-parameters
# alpha : community transmission rate
hhmodel <- hhmodel |>
  add_parameter("alpha",                # name matching the model source
                prior = "uniform",      # uniform prior
                proposal = "lognormal") # MCMC proposal

# beta : in-household person to person transmission rate
hhmodel <- hhmodel |>
  add_parameter("beta", prior = "uniform", proposal = "lognormal")
```

For a quick test, we can load parameter definitions directly from the template:

```{r}
#| label: load-parameter-template
# use housepi templated definitions
hhmodel <- hhmodel |>
  add_parameter_template()

# inspect current definitions
hhmodel |> 
  get_parameters()
```

We can also turn a parameter definition into a constant definition: it is sufficient to set the argument `const = TRUE`. In such case a `value` must be provided  .
To inspect current definitions, simply call `get_parameters` on the model object.

For further information on the available options for the definition of the parameter priors and MCMC proposal, see the vignette [Bayesian MCMC options](bayesian_mcmc_options.html).

# Run inference

After having provided all necessary definitions, we can perform inference calling `run_inference()`.
With housepi we can perform inference using Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) with the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm.
Standard options for the MCMC can be provided at this stage, including controls on the number of threads^[Multi-threading is implemented with *openMP* which is unfortunately not supported on latest macOS distributions.
The option `threads` is disabled on such systems.].
This will return an object which collects all the relevant MCMC draws.
The draws come as [posterior](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=posterior) objects that can be accessed to compute estimates.

```{r}
#| label: run-inference
# run the Monte Carlo specifying setup options
results <- hhmodel |>
  run_inference(steps = 2000, # MCMC steps per chain
                burn = 500,   # steps to drop before storing sample
                thin = 10,    # delay between stored samples
                adapt = 500,  # preliminary finite adaptation steps
                chains = 4,   # independent chains
                threads = 1)  # parallel threads

# summarize posterior draws of parameters
posterior::summarize_draws(get_parameter_draws(results))
```

# Inference and diagnostics

We can proceed as usual with other popular R packages for Bayesian analysis.
For example, we can extract the parameters draws by calling `get_parameter_draws` and plot traces with [bayesplot](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=bayesplot)

```{r}
#| label: param-traces
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plots for alpha and beta parameters across MCMC iterations with three parallel chains overlaid.
# visualize the traces of the first chain with 'bayesplot'
get_parameter_draws(results) |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace(facet_args = list(ncol = 1))
```

or of the total log-likelihood by calling `get_total_log_lik_draws`:

```{r}
#| label: log-lik-traces
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plots for total log-likelihood across MCMC iterations with three parallel chains overlaid.
get_total_log_lik_draws(results) |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace()
```

Similarly, we can call functions from [loo](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=loo).
We extract the sample of pointwise log-likelihood for each household and compute for example the leave-one-out cross-validation as follows

```{r}
#| label: loo-cv
# LOO-CV (leave-one-out cross-validation)
get_log_lik_draws(results) |>
  posterior::as_draws_matrix() |>
  loo::loo()
```

# Augmented infection times

For models requiring augmented variables, the definition procedure is analogous.
In [Data augmentation](data_augmentation.html) we broadly discuss data augmentation and the process of more complex augmented definitions.
Here we present a case study, using the template model "augmented_infection_time" where surveys are conditioned on single introduction.
We load the parameter definitions directly from the model template.

```{r}
#| label: load-augmented-model
# load a dataset for the data structure (used later for the simulation)
community_structure <- sarscov2_2021_icofs |>
  dplyr::select(id, house_id, age, sex) |>
  dplyr::mutate(status = NA, end_followup = 21)

hhsimul <- community_structure |>
  new_housepi_model("augmented_infection_time") |>
  add_parameter_template()

# inspect parameter definitions
get_parameters(hhsimul)
```

# Simulate an outbreak

We propose the following definitions for the augmented variables,
associated from a list by calling `add_augmented_list()`.

```{r}
#| label: load-augmented-definitions
hhsimul <- hhsimul |>
  add_augmented_list(
    # define default infection times of introduction cases
    # so that they all have symptom onset on day 0
    # secondary infection times are taken care by the simulation
    infec_time = - incub_period,

    # define an incubation period for each individual
    # arguments are linked to parameters
    incub_period = list(model = "gamma",
                        shape = inc_shape@P, scale = inc_scale@P,
                        max = 14)
  )
```

When dealing with many different nested definitions it is not unusual to lose track of which definitions are missing.
We can inspect the state of the current loaded model definitions just by printing the model:

```{r}
#| label: print-model-state
# print current state of definitions
hhsimul
```

This tells us that in order to proceed we need to provide the missing parameters which can be done appending to the existing ones via

```{r}
#| label: append-parameters
# append missing parameters for incubation period
hhsimul <- hhsimul |>
  add_parameter_list(inc_shape = 2, inc_scale = 1,
                      # set 'append' to TRUE to keep previous definitions
                      append = TRUE)
```

To see how to associate group rates in heterogeneous models, see the vignette [Group rates](group_rates.html).
However, by default if no group rate definition is provided all values are set to reference value 1, so we can forget about this alert for the rest of the walkthrough.
Similarly, we can use the infectivity profile template for the sake of demonstration.
Provide a custom definition following the vignette [Infectivity profiles](infectivity_profiles.html).

We then run a simulation with the method `run_simulation`, using the same community structure from the survey, but dropping cases.
In this configuration, introductions are sampled randomly.
Simulation will associate augmented incubation periods and onset times in addition to status.
We then propose a simple observation process, where we assume onsets after 6 PM (18/24) are reported to next day. We also want to drop unobserved quantities. We can do both by assigning such a function to the argument `obs_process`:

```{r}
#| label: run-simulation
# define an observation process after the outbreak simulation
obs_process <- function(x) {
  onset_date = floor(x$infec_time + x$incub_period + 0.25)
  x$onset_date <- ifelse(x$status > 0, onset_date, NA)
  x[!names(x) %in% c("incub_period", "infec_time")]
}

# run simulation using as structure the dataset associated at construction
simulated <- hhsimul |>
  run_simulation(obs_process = obs_process)

head(simulated)
```

# Validation

It is important to validate our approach checking that inference is able to recover the parameters used for the simulation, with a so called simulation study.


```{r}
#| label: inference-simulated
hhmodel <- simulated |>
  new_housepi_model("augmented_infection_time") |>
  add_parameter_template() |>
  add_parameter_list(inc_shape = 2, inc_scale = 1, append = TRUE) |>
  # loading definitions from list drops previous by default
  add_augmented_list(
    infec_time = onset_time - incub_period,
    onset_time = list(model = "normal", mean = onset_date@D, sd = 1),
    incub_period = list(model = "gamma",
                        shape = inc_shape@P, scale = inc_scale@P)
  )

results <- hhmodel |>
  run_inference(chains = 3, steps = 1000, adapt = 500, thin = 10)
```
We can visualize traces vs expected values as follows

```{r}
#| label: validation-traces
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plots for alpha, beta, and gamma parameters with three chains.
#|  Overlaying orange lines indicate the values used for the simulation.
library(ggplot2)

# extract sample to posterior draws_df
param_draws <- get_parameter_draws(results)

# select original parameters used for the simulation
simul_parameters <- get_parameters(hhsimul) |>
  dplyr::select(name, value) |>
  dplyr::filter(name %in% posterior::variables(param_draws)) |>
  dplyr::rename(parameter = name, simulated = value)

# use bayesplot to plot the posterior draws
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(param_draws, facet_args = list(ncol = 1)) +
  geom_hline(data = simul_parameters, aes(yintercept = simulated))
```

and we can perform R-hat diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: rhat-diagnostics
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-alt: >
#|  R-hat convergence diagnostics for alpha, beta, and gamma parameters with color-coded thresholds.
#|  Color intensity represents R-hat values (≤1.05, ≤1.1, >1.1). Points near 1.0 indicate convergence.
# compute Rhat values associated to inferred parameters
var_names <- get_parameters(hhmodel) |>
  dplyr::filter(!const) |>
  dplyr::pull(name)
rhat_values <- sapply(var_names, function(v) posterior::rhat(param_draws[[v]]))

# use bayesplot to showcase Rhat statistics
bayesplot::mcmc_rhat(rhat_values) +
  bayesplot::yaxis_text(hjust = 1)
```

Finally we wrap all together to compare to the parameters used for simulation.

```{r}
#| label: parameter-comparison-table
param_draws |>
  posterior::summarise_draws(
    median,
    ~posterior::quantile2(.x, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
  ) |>
  dplyr::reframe(parameter = variable,
                 inferred = format_credible_interval(
                   median, q2.5, q97.5, fmt = "%s (95%% CrI, %s-%s)")) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(simul_parameters, by = "parameter") |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::separate_header() |>
  flextable::bold(j = ~ parameter, bold = TRUE) |>
  flextable::autofit()
```

Due to the stochastic nature of this kind of simulation, limiting to re-infer parameters is a limiting check.
In [Posterior predictive checks](posterior_predictive_checks.html) we show how to compute common household measures according to the model posterior distribution.
